Excellent work to their team. If they do it again next year and you can attend, I recommend it.

Have we been too GENTLE with AI transformation?

At @every "After Automation" conference, folks from Anthropic ran a session on AI transformation. Someone asked about change management, and I feel like the answer was a bit too generic and hard to action IMHO.

So a few of us kept talking afterward.

I shared what we do at Optemization: run a design sprint, hear people out, let them walk us through their workflows so they’re invested in the process, and explain clearly why it’s worth it. Someone else said they run AI office hours, move slowly, and pick champions along the way.

Then a woman leading AI adoption at a company with 100,000+ employees said: “We tried all of that. None of it worked. So what now?”

Her answer was to go STERN. Adapt/learn or get left behind. Very Elon-esque I'd say. 

Kinda refreshing. Some people don’t want to be cradled.

But I’ve also seen people struggle with change and quietly disengage until someone teaches them. And AI is heavier than a new tool. The work someone spent years getting good at can suddenly be done by a machine. That hits their sense of identity and their place on the team.

Where do y'all land? When you push people toward AI, are you on the gentle or stern?

full_text:
One of the great pleasures of writing a book is getting to go on podcasts. (Seriously, this is like 40% of the reason to write a book.) And I've had a bunch of great conversations about The AGI Chronicles recently with people I admire. 

1. @asymmetricinfo and I got weird about the culture of AI, and whether Washington should nationalize the labs. https://t.co/KIocC5dsGX

2. Sam Harris and I talked for several very enjoyable hours for @MakingSenseHQ, of which about 22 minutes are available here (the rest is paywalled) https://t.co/FI6biTRr4j

3. I asked @reckless why he's not AGI-pilled, and he asked me why I am: https://t.co/FrMW76clnq

4. @ChristineEmba and I talked for Vox's "The Gray Area" about the ideologies driving the race for AGI. https://t.co/MM385DoIHJ

5. On the Vergecast, @pierce and I spent a solid 20 minutes talking about why Google missed the AI wave despite having invented most of the dang stuff in the first place. https://t.co/duhTVwcVdB

6. On Slate's What Next, @lizzieohreally2 and I talked about the underrated art of looking at straight lines on graphs and why I still save for retirement. 

7. On Semafor's Mixed Signals, @semaforben and @maxwelltani asked delightfully blunt questions about why I left the NYT and what the media gets wrong about AI. https://t.co/sO6oYNcgbq

8. @jordanschneider had me on ChinaTalk to talk through the analogies and disanalogies between AI and the Manhattan Project https://t.co/xGPiYCchr0

There are somehow more! (I am blessed to have a bizarre number of friends with great podcasts.) And I still have a few more stops on my book tour, like talking with @katelaurielee and @nxthompson at @every's Thesis conference on Friday. But I'm just emerging from a monthlong spirit quest of self-promotion and pinching myself at how many people I look up to actually seem to have read the book and gotten something out of it. It's extraordinarily gratifying, and almost makes the process of writing the fucking thing worth it. 

(Also: we need a podcast moratorium, this is getting crazy.)

full_text:
Human connection always wins.  Highlights from @every's panel with @nxthompson & @kevinroose today: 

Parasocial relationships with individual writers are the moat

"The Atlantic’s role will be to have individuals like an @anneapplebaum who you feel emotionally connected to because you feel like she understands the future and she understands democracy and we will want to build her audience while also creating enough gravity that she doesn’t go start her own YouTube channel where she would feel like she could make more money, have more influence if she does it without us."

"Part of what you are seeking to do is to build a parasocial relationship, a cult of personality, whatever you wanna call it, and then find ways to turn that into a distinct loyal audience and sell that to advertisers and subscribers."

Effort signaling (showing the work behind the work) matters more as AI content floods every channel

“If you’re an artist and you’re making something, in a computer program, you want to actually like film yourself on time-lapse making the thing and post that so that people know they can literally see the effort that went into it because we as just humans value things more highly when we believe that people put original thought and effort into something.”

Note to self: do this!

Attention scarcity is the real constraint

"If there's infinite music, the scarcity is the limited number of ears."

Emotional resonance keeps audiences loyal

People won't pay for more content, they'll pay for the specific feeling that one specific human is talking to them.

full_text:
Heading home from NY after @every Thesis conference, and the biggest takeaway was I expected to feel way behind. Instead, I felt less alone.

I met so many smart, chill people across product, engineering, design, and company leadership. Easily the most comfortable I’ve felt talking to people in a networking setting.

I expected to be blown away by everyone, and I was. But to my surprise, I was also right in the mix.

Loneliness came up often in conversation and even in some of the presentations. Many of us had been working through similar questions without many people around us to compare notes with.

It’s easy to interpret that isolation as being behind. Actually having those conversations changed that for me.

There was plenty of AI optimism, but also real discussion about what changes inside organizations. A recurring theme was how much more people can take on when they get good at working with AI, and how org design and incentive structures need to change around that.

How do you organize work when individuals can take on things that previously required a whole team?

In design conversations, I kept hearing a distinction between producing polished interfaces and deciding what should exist, how it should work, and how the pieces fit together.

Polish still matters. But as it becomes easier to produce, feelings were product and system judgment is where value creation is compounded. Makes me think how product design is currently evaluated might be a bit broken.

That connected with bets I’ve been making with my team. Changing how we design and ship, investing in the systems that let agents do useful work reliably, and making sure they have the right context before work starts.

I’ve had some self-doubt when explaining those investments and finding they don’t always click. I’d started wondering whether I had a communication problem.

These conversations helped me see that it isn’t just about finding better words. There’s a deeper enablement component too. People need opportunities to see these workflows in practice and build familiarity with what’s possible.

Helping create that shared understanding is part of my job.

Comparing notes with people working through similar problems gave me more confidence in the direction we’re taking. And honestly, it made me feel MUCH less crazy haha.

Really thankful to have been accepted, and already looking forward to next year!
